source.title: Scaling Is All You Need: Training Strong Policies for Autonomous Driving with JAX-Accelerated Reinforcement Learning
source.authors: Moritz Harmel; Anubhav Paras; Andreas Pasternak; Gary Linscott

record.file_problem: The full paper and supplementary material are present. Some cells in Figure 1’s flattened numeric layout are difficult to assign confidently to model-size and dataset-size combinations.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports scaling results for autonomous-driving reinforcement-learning policies, not language-model held-out cross-entropy or power-law fits. Its results do not test the listed claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports policy failure rates across model and dataset sizes, but these are a different measure and system from the claim’s language-model loss laws. The failure-rate findings are recorded under fits_no_version. Its simulator runtime benchmark, overall GPU-time estimates, SOTA comparison, and behavioral-cloning ablation do not test a claim version.
record.test_reason: The study trains autonomous-driving RL policies at three model sizes (0.75M–25M) and three dataset sizes (600–6000 h), with policy failure rate as the measure. It fits no power law, does not measure held-out loss, and studies no language models. It cites RL scaling laws and says it sees 'similar scaling behavior', which is discussion, not a test. Its 3×3 grid of failure rates cannot show a power-law form, so even V5 is not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that driving RL shows scaling behaviour similar to other RL settings, and that larger models help only with large enough real-world datasets. Their best policy (25M, 6000 h) cuts failure rate by 64% (to 0.88%) and improves progress by 25% versus the prior state of the art.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains autonomous-driving reinforcement-learning policies; it does not use or fit the language-model loss-scaling method.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported policy outcome varies with model size and dataset size. The authors state that increasing model size helps only when sufficient driving data is available.

fits_no_version.finding: In driving RL (BC then 2.5B PPO steps), minimum failure rate falls with dataset size at every model size. Model size helps only with enough data: 25M is worse than 2.5M at 2000 h and best at 6000 h (0.88%).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In real-data driving RL, policy failure rate improves with model and data scale, and gains from a larger model depend on dataset size.

record.problems: The reported results are autonomous-driving policy metrics rather than language-model loss measurements. No uncertainty estimates are reported for the scaling results. Figure 1’s flattened layout makes several model-by-dataset numeric assignments unclear.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted ambiguous Figure 1a cells for the 2.5M and 25M model rows rather than assigning their values to dataset conditions without clear layout support. Other performance and runtime results are outside the claim versions.

untested.parts: No language-model loss and no power-law fit in parameters, tokens or compute.
Only attention dimension varied; no shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
RL driving is another regime, but there is no loss measure and no power-law fit. Only three sizes per axis, with failure rate as the measure.
No exponents or fitting choices analysed.

missing.what: Three remaining Figure 1a cells, assignable using the text's constraints: 2.5M/2000 h ≈1.19%, 2.5M/6000 h ≈1.14%, 25M/2000 h ≈1.35%. Only this assignment fits the text: 2.5M strictly beats 0.75M, 25M is worse than 2.5M at 2000 h and better at 6000 h, and failure rate falls with data.
Figure 1b GPU time by model size: about 333–345 h for 0.75M, 805–975 h for 2.5M, 16118–18476 h for 25M. Dataset size has no effect on training time.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T6/discusses classification is kept. The grid values were inferred from a flattened figure using the text's qualitative statements. No uncertainty is reported, and each value is the best checkpoint selected on the evaluation set.

versions.untested_parts: Language-model held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute; no power-law fit.
No small-run fit or prediction of larger-run language-model loss.
No fixed-compute optimization of language-model parameter and token allocation.
No comparison of language-model architectures at fixed parameter count.
No test of whether the same power-law form holds for language-model loss in another modality or training regime.
The study evaluates autonomous-driving policy metrics, not language-model downstream-task performance or its relationship to pretraining loss.
No analysis of language-model scaling-law exponents, fitting choices, or departures from power-law curves.
